passages.t: Fire at the edge of the camp
passages.happening:
“Soon the people began to complain about their hardship in the hearing of the LORD, and when He heard them, His anger was kindled, and fire from the LORD blazed among them and consumed the outskirts of the camp” (verse 1).

The people cry out to Moses. Moses prays, and the fire dies down (verse 2). The place is named Taberah, which means burning (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 10 ended with the ark going ahead and Moses praying that God would rise up and return. Chapter 11 begins with complaint. The contrast is deliberate. The people who were counted, arranged, cleansed and given God's blessing in chapters 1 to 10 turn to grumbling within days.

These three verses are short, and they set a pattern that will repeat through chapter 21. The people complain. God's judgment falls. Someone prays for them. The judgment stops. And the place is given a name that remembers what happened.

Two details should be noticed. The fire burns at ‘the outskirts of the camp’, at its edge. It is a warning more than a destruction. And it stops when Moses prays. From the first complaint of the march, Moses stands between the people and what they have brought on themselves, and God listens to him.

The text does not say what the hardship was. The march through dry country was hard, and the book does not deny it. What it marks is the turn of the heart: after a year of God's care at Sinai, the first days of difficulty were met with complaint.
passages.later:
Moses later named this place among others when he reminded Israel of its record: “You continued to provoke the LORD at Taberah, at Massah, and at Kibroth-hattaavah” (Deuteronomy 9:22).

Paul tells the church at Philippi, “Do everything without complaining or arguing” (Philippians 2:14), in a passage that echoes Israel's wilderness years.
passages.asks: The first hard days of the road were met with complaint. Ask what you say, and to whom, in the first days of a difficulty. And ask who has prayed for you when you were in no state to pray for yourself.

passages.happening:
A craving for other food begins among ‘the rabble’ and spreads. The Israelites weep and say, ‘Who will feed us meat? We remember the fish we ate freely in Egypt, along with the cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic’ (verses 4-5). They are sick of the manna (verse 6).

Moses hears the weeping at the door of every tent, and he breaks. He asks God, “Why have You brought this trouble on Your servant?” (verse 11). “Did I conceive all these people?” he asks. Did he give them birth, that he should carry them like a nurse with a baby (verse 12)? “I cannot carry all these people by myself; it is too burdensome for me. If this is how You are going to treat me, please kill me right now” (verses 14-15).
passages.hearers:
The ‘rabble’ is a rare Hebrew word for a mixed crowd. It probably means the people who were not Israelites and left Egypt with Israel, the ‘mixed multitude’ of Exodus 12:38. The craving starts with them and soon belongs to everyone.

The foods they list were the everyday food of the Nile valley, where fish from the river and watered gardens fed even laborers. The memory is accurate as far as it goes. What it leaves out is the slavery. They ate ‘freely’, they say. Nothing in Egypt had been free.

The manna was not a poor food. It was gathered each morning, ground or pounded, and boiled or baked. “It tasted like pastry baked with fine oil” (verse 8). It was reliable, and it was enough. The people were simply tired of it. The complaint is not about hunger. It is about wanting something else, and wanting Egypt back.

Then the story turns to Moses, and it is one of the most honest pictures of a tired leader in the Bible. He does not pray a careful prayer. He accuses God. His picture is of a mother and a nurse: he did not give birth to this people, and he cannot be asked to carry them like a baby in arms. The words imply who did give them birth, and who should carry them.

The word for the weight he feels is ‘burden’, the same word used in chapter 4 for the loads the Levites carried. The man who assigned every Levite a load he could bear has been given one he cannot.

God does not rebuke Moses for this prayer. In the next passage he answers it with help.
passages.later:
Elijah prayed the same prayer under a broom tree: ‘I have had enough, LORD’ (1 Kings 19:4). God answered him with sleep, food and a companion.

In John's Gospel a crowd reminds Jesus that their ancestors ate manna in the wilderness. He answers, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger” (John 6:35).

Paul names this craving as a warning written for the church: “These things took place as examples to keep us from craving evil things as they did” (1 Corinthians 10:6).
passages.hard:
Moses asks God to kill him. Is that a sin? And what does his prayer say to someone who feels the same?

The text does not treat it as a sin. Moses says the worst of what he feels, and he says it to God. God's answer has no rebuke in it. He gives Moses seventy people to share the load. The Bible lets its strongest servants say that they have come to the end of themselves. Elijah said it too (1 Kings 19:4).

It should be noticed what God's answer was. He did not tell Moses to try harder or to have more faith. He said that Moses should not be carrying this alone, and he sent people.

So if your life is more than you can carry, that does not mean you are weak or that your faith has failed. People are not meant to carry it alone. The psalm says, “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18). Tell someone you trust: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. If you are thinking of ending your life, or you are in danger, get help now; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Israel remembered the fish and forgot the slavery. Ask what part of your own past you remember as better than it was, and what that false memory is doing to your trust in God now. And ask what load you are carrying alone that was never meant for one person.

passages.t: Seventy elders, and two men in the camp
passages.happening:
God answers Moses in two parts. For the burden: “Bring Me seventy of the elders of Israel” (verse 16). God will take some of the Spirit that is on Moses and put it on them. “They will help you bear the burden of the people, so that you do not have to bear it by yourself” (verse 17).

For the craving: the people will eat meat for a whole month, until they are sick of it, ‘because you have rejected the LORD, who is among you’ (verse 20). Moses cannot see how. There are 600,000 men on foot. God answers, “Is the LORD’s arm too short? Now you will see whether or not My word will come to pass” (verse 23).

The Spirit rests on the seventy and they prophesy (verse 25). Two of the men listed, Eldad and Medad, had stayed in the camp, and they prophesy there. Joshua says, “Moses, my lord, stop them!” (verse 28). “But Moses replied, ‘Are you jealous on my account? I wish that all the LORD’s people were prophets and that the LORD would place His Spirit on them!’” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is two stories woven together, the demand for meat and the burden of leading, and God answers both.

Elders were the heads of families and clans. They judged disputes and spoke for their people. The seventy were already known as leaders. God now fits them for a shared task by giving them the same Spirit that rested on Moses. Nothing in the passage suggests that Moses has less of the Spirit afterward. The gift is shared, and it is not used up.

God's words about the meat show what the complaint really was. The people had said, ‘Why did we ever leave Egypt?’ God calls that rejecting him. They were not asking for food. They were saying that the rescue had been a mistake.

Even Moses doubts. He has seen the sea part, and still he does the sums and finds them impossible. God's answer is a question. A short arm cannot reach. Is his arm short?

Then comes the scene with Eldad and Medad. Two men prophesy away from the tent, outside the gathering Moses called. A young man runs to report it. Joshua, who will one day lead Israel, wants it stopped. He is guarding Moses' honor.

Moses' reply is one of the finest things said by any leader in the Bible. He is not jealous of his position. He wishes that every one of God's people had the Spirit. A lesser man would have felt the two as rivals. In this chapter the same man who could not bear the people's weight turns out to have no wish to keep God's gifts to himself.

Verse 25 adds that the elders ‘never did so again’. The prophesying was a sign at their appointment. It was not their ongoing work.
passages.later:
The prophet Joel saw the day Moses wished for: “And afterward, I will pour out My Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy” (Joel 2:28). Peter quoted those words on the day of Pentecost, when the Spirit came on the whole church (Acts 2:17).

The disciples of Jesus once did what Joshua did. John said, “Teacher, we saw someone else driving out demons in Your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not accompany us” (Mark 9:38). Jesus answered, “Do not stop him” (Mark 9:39).

Before another meal in a lonely place the disciples asked Moses' question: “Where in this desolate place could anyone find enough bread to feed all these people?” (Mark 8:4).
passages.asks: Moses was glad to see the Spirit rest on men outside his own meeting. Ask how you feel when God plainly uses someone outside your group, your church or your way of doing things. And ask where you have done the sums, like Moses, and decided that what God has said cannot be done.

passages.t: Quail, and the graves of craving
passages.happening:
A wind from the LORD drives quail in from the sea. They fall around the camp, thick on the ground, as far as a day's walk in every direction (verse 31). The people gather them for two days and a night. No one gathers less than ten homers (verse 32).

“But while the meat was still between their teeth, before it was chewed, the anger of the LORD burned against the people, and the LORD struck them with a severe plague” (verse 33).

“So they called that place Kibroth-hattaavah, because there they buried the people who had craved other food” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
The detail fits the region. Quail cross the Sinai in spring and autumn as they travel between Africa and the lands to the north. They often fly low and land worn out after crossing the sea, and then they can be caught in great numbers. Israel left Sinai in the second month, which falls in spring.

The Hebrew word for the wind here, ruach, is the same word used a few verses earlier for the Spirit on the elders. One word names the gift that fitted leaders to serve and the power that brought the judgment.

The quantity is enormous. A homer was a large dry measure, and ten of them was far more than any household could eat. The people did not gather to meet a need. They heaped up.

The name of the place means the graves of craving. It is the second name of the chapter. The first meant burning. Both names are warnings left on the map.

The plague is troubling, and the hard question below takes it up.
passages.later: The Psalms remember the day with a hard sentence: “So He granted their request, but sent a wasting disease upon them” (Psalm 106:15). Psalm 78 tells the same story at length (Psalm 78:26-31).
passages.hard:
Why would God give the people meat and then strike them with a plague while they were still eating?

The scene is hard, and the text does not soften it.

The chapter's own explanation is that the trouble was never hunger. The people had manna every day. Their demand was a rejection of God, who was among them, and a wish that they had never left Egypt (verse 20). The plague is said to fall on ‘the people who had craved’ (verse 34). The judgment answers contempt for the rescue. It does not answer need.

Some interpreters have suggested a natural cause. Quail that have fed on certain plants can make people who eat them seriously ill, and this has been known since ancient times. The text does not describe how the plague came. It says only that it came from God's anger.

The Psalms took the story as a warning that God may give people what they demand and let them find out what it costs.

None of this makes the story easy. It was a judgment at one moment in Israel's beginning, told as a warning, and it must not be turned on anyone who suffers today.

A word of care. This story must not be used to say that a sudden death, an accident or an illness today is God's punishment on the person who suffered it. Jesus refused that kind of reasoning: of people killed when a tower fell, he asked, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you have lost someone suddenly, or carry fear or guilt after reading this, please speak with someone you trust, a pastor or a friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The people were given exactly what they demanded, and it did them no good. Ask what you have been demanding from God for a long time, and whether you have asked what it would do to you to get it. And ask what daily bread you have stopped being thankful for because it comes every day.
